title: Pawn races
summary: Count the tempi, queen with check and make the new queen work before the other one does.
part.count.title: Counting the tempi
part.count.summary: Who queens first, and why that is only enough when the new queen does something on the very next move.
part.check.title: Queening with check
part.check.summary: A queen born with check wins the tempo you need to stop the other pawn.
part.control.title: The newly promoted queen
part.control.summary: The long diagonal watches the other queening square; and, with two queens on the board, the skewering check.
part.catch.title: Race or hunt
part.catch.summary: Sometimes the king catches the pawn and there is no race at all. And the king never waits on the other queen's line.
part.behind.title: When the pawn reaches the seventh
part.behind.summary: A bishop's pawn on the seventh still saves the game, as in Petrosian–Fischer. Then the rules and a game.
step.t_race: Both pawns are passed and neither king can reach the other pawn. White to move. Count each side's moves to promotion. Who queens first, and is that enough?
step.t_race.hint1: The h2 pawn may advance two squares on its first move. Count how many moves it needs to reach h8, and how many the a7 pawn needs to reach a1.
step.t_race.hint2: Both of them queen. Look at the diagonal that starts on h8 and see where it ends.
step.square: First, the usual question: can either king step into the square of the other pawn? The black king on b5 is far from the square of the h2 pawn, and my king on f4 is far from the square of the a7 pawn. So it is a real race: each side pushes its own pawn.
step.tempo: Now count. With h4, my pawn needs five moves to queen: h4, h5, h6, h7, h8. The black pawn also needs five: a5, a4, a3, a2, a1. I move first, so I queen first. That alone does not win: queen against queen is usually a draw. What wins is that my queen on h8 watches a1 along the diagonal. With h3 I would lose a tempo, both queens would appear and it would be a draw.
step.d_race: Watch the whole race. Count with me, move by move.
step.d_race.m1: h4: the double step. That is what puts me a tempo ahead.
step.d_race.m2: Black races too. The black king has nowhere useful to go.
step.d_race.m8: a2. The black pawn will queen as well.
step.d_race.m9: h8, queen. Look at the diagonal: from h8 to a1, nothing in the way.
step.d_race.m10: Black queens, but the new queen lands on a square I already control.
step.d_race.m11: Queen takes a1. The black queen lived for one move. Now it is queen against king.
step.raceMove: Your turn. White to move and win. Do the count and race with the right pawn in the right way.
step.raceMove.hint: Do not waste time: the h2 pawn can move two squares. And no king move helps here.
step.raceMove.done: That's it. You stay a tempo ahead, and the queen will be born on h8, eyeing a1.
step.t_check: White to move. Both pawns run, and neither king can reach the other pawn. Count, then look at where the black king stands. What can the white queen do the moment it is born?
step.t_check.hint1: The a4 pawn queens on a8. Trace the diagonal from a8 to h1 and see who is on it.
step.t_check.hint2: Queening with check gains a move. With that move, the queen reaches the square where the black pawn wants to queen.
step.checkWhy: The black king is on f3, on the long diagonal. When my pawn queens on a8, the queen arrives with check. Black spends the move on the king, and I use mine to put the queen on h1, in front of the black pawn. Queening with check is worth a tempo.
step.d_check: See how the check decides a race that the count alone would call even.
step.d_check.m1: a5. My pawn needs three more moves. The black one needs four, but it is Black's turn now.
step.d_check.m6: h2. If the white queen were born without check, Black would queen next move.
step.d_check.m7: a8, queen, with check along the diagonal. Black has no time to queen.
step.d_check.m8: The king steps out of check and stays near the pawn to protect it.
step.d_check.m9: Queen to h1, in front of the pawn. It will never queen, and my king comes to collect it at leisure.
step.checkMove: White to move and win. The black pawn is one step from queening. Use the check.
step.checkMove.hint: Queen on the square where the new queen gives check at once. Then stop the black pawn on its queening square.
step.checkMove.done: Perfect. The queen was born with check and went to h1. Now the white king walks over and the pawn falls.
step.t_control: White to move. The black pawn is on a2, one step from becoming a queen, and the white king cannot get there. White still wins. How?
step.t_control.hint1: A queen on h8 sees right across the board along the long diagonal.
step.controlWhy: The black pawn will queen on a1, and a1 is on the same diagonal as h8. If I queen on h8, the new queen watches a1: when the black pawn promotes, I take its queen. One detail: it has to be a queen. A bishop would also take the queen on a1, but king and bishop alone cannot mate: a draw.
step.d_skewer: Another way the new queen can work: the skewering check. Here both sides queen, one after the other, and neither queen watches the other's square. Watch what happens next.
step.d_skewer.m2: b2. Black is one move away as well.
step.d_skewer.m4: b1, queen. Two queens on the board. It looks drawn, but look at the b-file.
step.d_skewer.m5: Queen to b8, check. The black king is on b5 and, behind it on the same file, the black queen.
step.d_skewer.m6: The king has to leave the file.
step.d_skewer.m7: And the queen on b1 falls. The check went straight through the king, like a skewer.
step.controlMove: Now you. White to move and win. The black pawn will queen no matter what: make your queen appear with its eye on that square.
step.controlMove.hint: Promote to a queen, not a bishop or a rook. Then take whatever appears on a1.
step.controlMove.done: Yes. The queen on h8 watched a1 from its very first move. The black queen lasted one move.
step.t_catch: White to move. Both pawns are passed. Before you count who queens first, think: do you really have to race?
step.t_catch.hint1: The black king is on h7. Can it step into the square of the a4 pawn?
step.t_catch.hint2: And the white king: how many moves does it need to get in front of the f4 pawn?
step.catchWhy: If I race with a5, both pawns queen and it is queen against queen: a draw. But my king on b3 can reach the f4 pawn, while the black king on h7 cannot reach my a4 pawn. So I hunt first: Kc3, Kd2, Ke2 and the f-pawn falls. After that my pawn walks in alone. Before racing, always check whether your king can catch the other pawn.
step.catchMove: White to move and win. Take the king to the f-pawn, and don't hurry with the a-pawn.
step.catchMove.hint: The f4 pawn will queen on f1. Head for e2 or f1 with the king, along the lower ranks.
step.catchMove.done: Exactly. The king caught the pawn, and the black king will never reach your a-pawn. Hunting beat racing.
step.diagonal: Now the other side: you are Black. The count favours you, but look at your king on d5, on the a8–h1 diagonal. If you race the pawn all the way, White queens on a8 with check and takes your queen on h1 along the same line. The way out is to step off the diagonal with the king and, while you are at it, go after the a-pawn.
step.diagonalMove: Black to move and win. The first move may be the pawn's; after that, mind the diagonal.
step.diagonalMove.hint: After h3 and a6, do not carry on with h2. The black king leaves the diagonal and heads for the a-pawn.
step.diagonalMove.done: Well done. The king left the diagonal and caught the pawn. Racing on with h2 would have lost to a8=Q+.
step.t_fischer: Now you are the one who arrives late. Black to move. White will queen first and nothing can stop it. Can the game still be saved?
step.t_fischer.hint1: Your pawn is a bishop's pawn. Bring it to the seventh with the king beside it, and think about the corner.
step.fischer: This position comes from Petrosian against Fischer, 1958: they agreed a draw because the analysis showed this. White queens first, but the black pawn reaches the seventh with its king alongside. A bishop's pawn on the seventh, with its king nearby and the white king far away, draws against the queen: when the queen takes the pawn, the black king is stalemated in the corner. Whoever loses the race still runs, with the right pawn.
step.d_fischer: Watch the defence. You play Black; notice where the king ends up.
step.d_fischer.m1: Kb1. The king goes next to the pawn without blocking c2.
step.d_fischer.m2: White queens. Now it is queen against pawn.
step.d_fischer.m3: c2. The pawn reaches the seventh, guarded by the king.
step.d_fischer.m4: Check. The queen wants to drive the king in front of its pawn.
step.d_fischer.m5: Ka2. The king steps out of check and stays close.
step.d_fischer.m9: Ka1! The king goes into the corner, not in front of the pawn.
step.d_fischer.m10: The queen took the pawn, and Black has no move at all: stalemate. The white king was too far away to help.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: count each pawn's moves, with the double step and the turn, and see whether either king gets into the square; if your king can catch the pawn, hunt before you race. Second: queening first only wins if the new queen does something on the very next move: give check, watch the other queening square, or skewer the other queen. Third: never leave your king on the line of the other side's future queen.
step.finish: Now play it to the end. Count, queen first and put the queen to work.
ex.e11: White to move and win. The race is over: both queens are on the board, and it is White to move.
ex.e11.hint: The black king is on the a-file and its queen is on b1. Which file can a check force the king onto?
ex.e11.solution: Qa8+! The king only has squares on the b-file (Kb4, Kb5 or Kb6), and then Qb8+ (Qb7+ works too) is a skewer: the king leaves the file and Qxb1. Had Black been to move, Black would have traded the queens. Position from the study "Pawn Races" by njswift.
ex.e12: Black to move and draw. Najdorf–Vinueza, 1941. White threatens Ke2 to stop your pawn. Where does your king go?
ex.e12.hint: The white pawn will queen on b8. Which diagonal leaves b8? Then think about what saves a bishop pawn when the queen is born first.
ex.e12.solution: Kh3! On g3 the king would stand on the b8–h2 diagonal, and the new queen would arrive with check; f4 also loses. After b5, f4, and when the white king comes with Ke4, Kg3! The bishop pawn reaches the second rank with its king beside it, and with the white king far away the queen cannot win (the bishop-pawn stalemate, as in Petrosian–Fischer).
ex.e13: Black to move and win. Running with the pawn right away looks natural. What does the white king want to do?
ex.e13.hint: The white king wants to come back along the long diagonal to catch the f-pawn. Who closes its path?
ex.e13.solution: Kd5! After f5? the white king comes back with Kb4 and Kc3 and arrives in time. After Kb4, Kd4! The white king stands in front of its own pawn and has no way back; then f5 (or Kd5) and the race belongs to Black. At the end the white king lands on f1's diagonal, and f1=Q+ arrives with check and wins the other queen. Position from the study "Pawn Races" by njswift.
ex.e14: White to move and win. Nesterov–Zolnierowicz, 1993. Both kings stand in front of their pawns. Which king move?
ex.e14.hint: Both sides will queen. Think about what the white queen does right after the black one appears on b1, and about the h-pawn that remains.
ex.e14.solution: Ke5! (Ke4 and Kf5 draw.) The pawn runs and queens first: f4, f5, f6, f7, f8=Q, and after b1=Q the checks Qc5+, Qf2+, Qd4+ and Qb6+ drive the black king until the queen on b1 falls or is traded (Qxb1+). What is left is a pawn ending in which the white king, close to the h-pawn, wins.
ex.e15: White to move and win. Study by Grigoriev, 1931. Black has an extra pawn. Only one move wins, and then two more.
ex.e15.hint: The black pawns can move two squares. And when the white pawn queens on g8, which diagonal is the black king on a2 sitting on?
ex.e15.solution: h4! keeps the black pawns together, within reach of the king (h3 draws). After h5, Kf8! and not Kf7: the king must stay off the a2–g8 diagonal and off the g-file. After g6, Ke7! (Kf7, Kg7, Ke8 and Kg8 draw). Then g5, hxg5, h4, g6, h3, g7, h2 and g8=Q+: the queen is born checking the king on a2 and gets there before the h-pawn.
ex.e16: White to move and win. Study by Grigoriev, 1931. White is ahead, but every move has to be exact.
ex.e16.hint: The a-pawn can move two squares, sometimes with check. Which squares should the white king avoid, and along which path does it reach b7?
ex.e16.solution: c4! and c5! The pawn moves before the black king arrives (Kc5? blocks its own pawn). Then the king zigzags: Ka5!, Ka6! and only then Kb5!, when the black king can no longer go to d5. On b5 too early comes a6+ or Kd5. After Kc6 and Kb7 both sides queen, but c8=Q a1=Q Qh8+ skewers along the long diagonal and the queen on a1 falls.
ex.e17: White to move and win. Study by Khachaturov, 1947, on an idea by Grigoriev. Two pawns against two, and every move is the only one.
ex.e17.hint: Make the black king spend moves. Where does the f-pawn queen, and what happens if the black king is on the eighth rank when the h-pawn arrives?
ex.e17.solution: f5! (the f-pawn would queen with check), and after Kc5, h5! After g3, Ke1! (Ke2? allows d3 with check). The technique: every time the black king moves, a white pawn advances: f6, h6, Kf2, f7, h7. After g1=Q+ Kxg1 d2, f8=Q+! offers the queen: Kxf8 and h8=Q+ is born with check and arrives in time to stop the d-pawn.
ex.e18: White to move and draw. Study by Moravec, 1950. Taking the d-pawn at once looks obvious. Is it?
ex.e18.hint: Count until Black queens on e1 and the white king goes to c8. Where does the deciding check come from, and who can block that line?
ex.e18.solution: Kd5! After Kxd6? e4, c4 e3, c5 e2, c6 e1=Q, Kd7 Qd1+ Kc8 and Qg4+ wins. Kd5 threatens Ke4 to stop the e-pawn, and the black king comes to f3: after Kxd6 and the same race (Kd7 Qd1+ Kc8), the black king on f3 blocks the d1–g4 diagonal and the c-pawn holds the draw.
key.race: Both pawns queen, but White gets there first, and the new queen in the corner already watches the square where the black pawn wants to queen. Counting is not enough: you must see what the queen does next.
key.check: The white pawn queens with check, because the black king stands on the same diagonal as the queening square. With that extra move, the queen is in time to stop the other pawn.
key.control: The white pawn queens in the corner, and the new queen controls the black pawn's queening square from afar. Promoting to anything but a queen would throw the win away.
key.skewer: Both sides queen and there are two queens on the board. A check along the line of Black's king and queen skewers the king, and the queen behind it falls.
key.catch: Running is not always best: here the white king first hunts down the black pawn, and the white edge pawn then queens on its own, because the black king is too far away.
key.diagonal: Black cannot simply run: if the pawn goes all the way, White queens with check. The black king must turn back and capture the white pawn first.
key.petrosianFischer: Petrosian against Fischer, 1958: both sides were about to queen, but Black's bishop pawn would reach the last square but one with its king beside it. The queen cannot win against that, and they agreed a draw.
key.alatortsev: Alatortsev against Chekhover, 1937: Black's bishop pawn was still one square further back. That square gave the queen time to bring the white king closer, and White won.
history: In a pawn race each side has a free pawn and both run to queen. It seems to be just a matter of counting squares, and many players lose here by counting wrong or stopping too soon: whoever queens first may still not win, and whoever queens second sometimes loses the new queen to a check. The basic tool is the rule of the square, which every endgame book teaches. In 1958 Petrosian and Fischer, two future world champions, agreed a draw in an ending like this, because Fischer's pawn would get too close to queening for the queen to win. In 1937 Alatortsev beat Chekhover in a similar race, because there the pawn was one square further back. One square made all the difference.
practice: Now the real ending: an a-pawn against a g-pawn, with the black king on f3. Count, race with the double step and use the check when the queen is born. Pick your time control and go.
